action_criteria.expected_evidence: Complex fasciculation potentials in cervical and lumbosacral muscles without definite fibrillation potentials or chronic neurogenic change; no conduction block; normal sensory studies; repeat study recommended.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal brain MRI: no structural, demyelinating or vascular lesion and no corticospinal tract signal change.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cervical and thoracic spine MRI: no cord compression or cord signal change.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 420 U/L (2.4x ULN); blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 92% predicted and SNIP 88 cmH2O, within normal limits: an objective baseline only.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP) as an objective baseline while ALS is not established
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function neither supports nor excludes ALS. In a symptomatic SOD1 carrier without respiratory or bulbar symptoms it only provides an objective baseline for follow-up, so it is optional.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Heterozygous pathogenic SOD1 c.14C>T, p.(Ala5Val) (A4V) variant; C9orf72, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1 negative. Carrier status is a genetic risk, not a diagnosis.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. The death of his paternal uncle from ALS at 52 makes a monogenic cause in the family likely; testing after pre-test counselling defines his genetic risk and that of his relatives, and a SOD1 result determines eligibility for gene-targeted treatment once ALS is established, or for trials.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start riluzole or tofersen before ALS is established clinically and electrodiagnostically.
Do not attribute the symptoms to detraining or anxiety without the repeat EMG and review.
required_recommendations: Explain that the SOD1 A4V variant is pathogenic and that ALS is suspected but not established, and arrange post-test genetic counselling.
Offer counselling to his first-degree relatives, each of whom has a 50% chance of carrying the variant, with predictive testing only after counselling.
Record an objective neurological baseline (MRC grades in named muscles, reflexes, ALSFRS-R), interpreted against his athletic baseline.
Complete brain and spine MRI and the blood tests for mimic exclusion before any ALS-specific treatment decision.
Repeat EMG/NCS in 6 to 8 weeks with clinical review, looking for active denervation, spread and definite upper motor neuron signs.
Refer to a specialist ALS centre now so that tofersen can be discussed as soon as ALS is established, and trials for SOD1 carriers considered.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

accepted: Suspected early ALS in a SOD1 A4V pathogenic-variant carrier, Gold Coast criteria not yet met

differential.diagnosis: Benign fasciculations with detraining atrophy in a former athlete
differential.key_features: supports: fasciculations are common after intense training, calf bulk loss since retiring 2 years ago, near-normal strength, no definite active denervation or chronic neurogenic change on EMG; against: complex fasciculation morphology in two regions, an interval rise in reflexes from 2+ to 3+, and a pathogenic SOD1 A4V variant

differential.diagnosis: Hereditary spastic paraparesis with motor neuron involvement
differential.key_features: supports: brisk reflexes; against: no spasticity, flexor plantar responses, normal gait, prominent fasciculations, and the SOD1 result explains the family history

differential.diagnosis: Kennedy disease (spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy)
differential.key_features: against: normal sensory responses (SBMA is a pure lower motor neuron disorder with sensory neuronopathy), no bulbar involvement, and an X-linked disease cannot pass from a paternal uncle through the father to a son; the androgen receptor CAG repeat was not tested
against: widespread proximal and distal fasciculations, brisk reflexes, normal CMAP amplitudes, and a pathogenic SOD1 variant that explains the family history

key_clinical_evidence: SOD1 A4V (p.Ala5Val) is an aggressive variant, typically with lower motor neuron-predominant onset and short survival, so a symptomatic carrier needs close surveillance.

Carrier status does not establish ALS: Gold Coast 2020 needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in two, after other diseases are excluded. Neither is documented yet.
Upper motor neuron evidence is currently equivocal: reflexes have risen from 2+ to 3+, but there are no Hoffman or Babinski signs and no spasticity.

EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change. This study shows complex fasciculations without definite chronic neurogenic change or fibrillation potentials.

Serial examination and a repeat EMG in 6 to 8 weeks decide: spread of complex fasciculations with fibrillation potentials and chronic neurogenic change, or definite upper motor neuron signs, would establish ALS.

Tofersen is authorised only for ALS with a SOD1 pathogenic variant (FDA accelerated approval 2023, EU authorisation 2024); starting it is a specialist-centre decision once ALS is established, not a treatment for carrier status, and presymptomatic treatment of carriers is studied only in trials.
CK 420 U/L (2.4x ULN) is a non-specific mild rise: it is common in ALS from denervation and also follows exercise, and it does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fasciculations are common in athletes and calf bulk falls with detraining, but complex fasciculations in two regions, an interval rise in reflexes and a pathogenic SOD1 A4V variant require close follow-up and a repeat EMG rather than reassurance.
red_herrings.data_point: Former elite swimmer with calf bulk loss since retiring 2 years ago
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent to dismiss the calf wasting and fasciculations as detraining and exercise-related

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Relative hyperreflexia without Hoffman or Babinski signs or spasticity is equivocal upper motor neuron evidence; with no definite active denervation on EMG, Gold Coast criteria are not yet met.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent to count relative hyperreflexia as definite upper motor neuron involvement and diagnose ALS

sequence_constraints.reason: Genetic testing follows the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment and pre-test counselling; it does not make the diagnosis.

findings.finding: Right first dorsal interosseous: complex fasciculation potentials (polyphasic, duration over 5 ms). No fibrillation potentials or positive sharp waves. Motor unit potentials at the upper limit of normal for amplitude and duration, stable, with full recruitment.

Both gastrocnemii and tibialis anterior: complex fasciculation potentials. No definite fibrillation potentials. Right tibialis anterior: possible sparse positive sharp waves, of uncertain significance.
Thoracic paraspinals: no abnormal spontaneous activity.
Fasciculation potentials in the cervical and lumbosacral muscles are complex (high amplitude, polyphasic, long duration), distinguishable from simple fasciculation potentials.

Median, ulnar, peroneal and tibial motor studies: CMAP amplitudes within normal limits, in the lower part of the reference range; distal latencies and conduction velocities normal; no conduction block.
Median, ulnar and sural sensory responses normal.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Complex fasciculation potentials in the cervical (right first dorsal interosseous) and lumbosacral (gastrocnemii, tibialis anterior) segments. 2. No definite fibrillation potentials; possible sparse positive sharp waves in the right tibialis anterior, of uncertain significance. 3. Motor unit potentials at the upper limit of normal in the right first dorsal interosseous; no definite chronic neurogenic change. 4. Thoracic paraspinal and bulbar muscles normal. 5. Normal motor conduction with no conduction block; normal sensory studies. The findings are of uncertain significance: complex fasciculations without definite active denervation or chronic neurogenic change. Repeat study in 6-8 weeks recommended.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: A paternal uncle with ALS, a former athlete's baseline and an EMG of uncertain significance: the pathogenic SOD1 result must not be mistaken for a diagnosis of ALS, and treatment waits for the disease to be established.
metadata.notes: SOD1 A4V pathogenic-variant carrier with suspected early ALS in a former elite athlete. Equivocal upper motor neuron evidence and an EMG with complex fasciculations but no definite denervation: Gold Coast criteria are not yet met. The case turns on post-test and cascade counselling, an objective baseline, repeat EMG and early referral to a specialist centre, with tofersen deferred until ALS is established.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. C is a 45-year-old retired professional swimmer who presents with a 6-month history of widespread muscle fasciculations and subtle weakness. He noticed fasciculations first in his calves 6 months ago, and they have spread to his thighs and both arms. He recently learned that his paternal uncle died of ALS at age 52, which has caused him significant anxiety.

He reports mild weakness compared with his athletic baseline: he can no longer swim his usual training distances without unusual fatigue, and his performance in gym workouts has fallen. He notes an apparent reduction in calf bulk on both sides. He has no swallowing, speech or sensory symptoms.

He retired from competitive swimming 2 years ago and has trained much less since then. His primary care physician recorded biceps and knee reflexes of 2+ at a routine examination before the symptoms began.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No tongue fasciculations. No dysarthria.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Athletic habitus. Worried.
neurological_exam.motor: Fasciculations visible in bilateral thighs, calves, and both arms at rest. Muscle bulk appears reduced bilateral calves vs expected for former athlete. Strength tests: appears near-normal 4+/5 to 5-/5 throughout — submaximal effort difficult to exclude given anxiety. No clear focal weakness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally (previously documented 2+ by PCP). Brachioradialis 3+. Knee jerks 3+ (previously 2+). No Hoffman. No Babinski — plantar responses flexor.
